title: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS” — THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES WITHOUT STARTING AT EPHESIANS 5:21
paragraphs: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS” — THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES WITHOUT STARTING AT EPHESIANS 5:21

Before a husband ever gets to quote “submit,” Scripture has already placed him beneath the cross—and what Paul actually wrote may confront both husbands and wives more deeply than the isolated verse ever could.
There is a sentence from the Bible that has entered more marriage arguments than some marriage counselors.
“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands…”
Some men know those words by heart.
They can find Ephesians 5:22 faster than they can find the last place their wife quietly cried because she felt unheard.

Some women hear those words and immediately tense up—not necessarily because they hate Scripture, not because they reject God, but because somewhere along the way somebody may have used a holy verse with an unholy spirit.
A command meant to live beneath the shadow of Jesus Christ became a weapon.
A passage about Christlike marriage became a slogan about male control.
And sometimes the tragedy is not that the Bible was quoted incorrectly.
The tragedy is that somebody started reading one verse too late.
Because before Paul addresses wives in Ephesians 5:22, there is Ephesians 5:21.
And that changes the atmosphere of the entire conversation.
The Greek reads:
“ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ.”
Hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
In straightforward English:
“Submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
Before Paul speaks directly to wives…
before husbands are addressed…
before marriage roles become the discussion…
Christ is already standing in the middle of the room.
And everybody has to bow.
The Greek matters here.

The word translated “submitting” in verse 21 is hypotassomenoi, from hypotassō—to subject oneself, to place oneself in an ordered relationship, to submit. But notice something fascinating about the flow of the Greek text.
In an important stream of the earliest Greek textual tradition reflected in modern critical editions, verse 22 does not repeat an explicit verb for “submit.” It reads essentially:
“Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ…”
“The wives to their own husbands as to the Lord…”
The idea of submission carries forward grammatically from the preceding statement.
That does not erase verse 22.
It does not make the instruction to wives disappear.
It does not allow us to rewrite Paul because modern culture finds his words uncomfortable.
But it does force us to stop pretending verse 22 dropped out of heaven without verse 21 standing immediately before it.

Paul has been describing Spirit-filled Christian life. He tells believers to be filled with the Spirit, to worship, to give thanks—and then to live in a posture of submission toward one another out of reverence for Christ.
Then he turns toward the household.
The question is no longer merely:
“Woman, are you submitting?”
The uncomfortable question becomes:
“Is anybody in this marriage behaving like Jesus?”
Because Paul does tell wives to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord.
We should not be embarrassed by Scripture.
We should understand it faithfully.
But then Paul turns toward the husband.
And husbands…
you may want to sit down for this.
Because Paul never says:
“Husbands, make sure your wives submit.”
He does not tell the husband to enforce submission.
He gives the husband another command.
A terrifying one.
A crucifying one.
A command that leaves very little room for selfish masculinity.
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας…”
“Husbands, love your wives…”
And then comes the standard.
Not according to your mood.
Not according to whether she agrees with you.
Not according to whether dinner was made.
Not according to whether she gave you the respect you think you deserved.
Not according to what the men in your family taught you masculinity looked like.
Paul points to Jesus.
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν…”
“Just as Christ loved the church…”
And what did Christ do?
“καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“He gave Himself up for her.”
There it is.
The cross.
That is where biblical husbandhood goes to die to itself.
The husband wants to talk about headship?
Paul points him toward a bloody Savior.
The husband wants authority?
Paul shows him Christ giving Himself away.
The husband wants to know what leadership looks like?
Look at Jesus.
Look at the One washing feet.
Look at the One touching lepers.
Look at the One welcoming children.
Look at the One carrying burdens.
Look at the One enduring betrayal.
Look at the One who could summon angels but stretched out His hands instead.
Look at Calvary.

Christian headship can never faithfully be used as a theological costume for selfishness, intimidation, humiliation, manipulation, violence, or domination because the model Paul gives the husband is Christ Himself.
And Christ “gave Himself up for her.”
That means a man cannot scream, “Submit to me!” while refusing to die to his pride and imagine that Ephesians 5 is on his side.
Brother…
before asking whether your wife respects your leadership, ask what your leadership is costing you.
Does she experience your strength as safety?
Can she disagree without fearing punishment?
Can she tell you that you hurt her without watching your ego immediately build a courtroom?
Do you listen?
Do you repent?
Do you apologize without adding, “but you…”
Do you pray for her?
Do you protect her dignity when she is not in the room?
Do you know what has been exhausting her lately?
Do you notice what she carries?
When was the last time you asked what her heart needed and stayed quiet long enough to hear the answer?
Because Jesus did not love the Church merely by announcing His position over her.
He gave Himself for her.
And wife…
Scripture speaks to you too.
Biblical submission is not inferiority.
The passage never says a woman is less intelligent, less valuable, less human, less spiritually significant, or somehow farther from God.
Your husband is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
Your husband is not your mediator.
Jesus is.
Your husband is not your ultimate Lord.
Jesus is.
And the words “as to the Lord” can never legitimately mean “obey a husband instead of the Lord.”
No human authority gets permission to overrule God.
The apostles themselves established the principle when commanded to violate allegiance to God: “We must obey God rather than men.”
So submission cannot mean becoming an accomplice to sin.
It cannot mean calling evil good.
It cannot mean protecting criminal behavior.
It cannot mean that a battered woman must quietly endure violence because leaving immediate danger would somehow disappoint Jesus.
It cannot mean surrendering conscience to another sinner.
And if someone has used Ephesians 5 to convince you that abuse is holiness, please hear this carefully:
Jesus does not need your destruction to prove His Word is true.
Sin remains sin even when the sinner knows Bible verses.
At the same time, we must resist the opposite temptation.
We cannot rescue Scripture from abuse by deleting whatever Scripture says that our culture dislikes.
Christian marriage is not built on two autonomous people protecting themselves from ever having to yield.
It is built on two people who belong first to Jesus Christ.
A Christian wife is called to a real posture of respect and submission toward her own husband.
A Christian husband is commanded to love his wife with the staggering pattern of Christ's self-giving love.
And both stand under the lordship of Jesus.
That is why Ephesians 5:21 matters so much.
“Submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.”
Mutual submission does not necessarily mean every relationship or responsibility becomes identical. Paul goes on to address wives and husbands distinctly. We should let him.
But neither can those distinct instructions be separated from the Spirit-filled, Christ-revering posture Paul has just established.
The wife cannot say, “His responsibility to love means I never have to yield.”
The husband cannot say, “Her responsibility to submit means I get to dominate.”
Both arguments smell suspiciously like the same thing:
self.
And Jesus came to put self on a cross.
Maybe that is why this passage hurts when we actually read all of it.
Because it is much easier to use Scripture to diagnose your spouse than to let Scripture perform surgery on you.
“Husbands, she needs to submit.”
“Wives, he needs to love.”
And Jesus stands between both accusations asking:
“What about you?”
What if tonight you stopped reading Ephesians 5 as ammunition?
What if you read it as a mirror?
Imagine the husband who has quoted verse 22 for years suddenly reaching verse 25 and realizing:
“My wife isn't the only person God is confronting.”
Imagine him putting down the Bible he had been using to win the argument.
Imagine him walking into the kitchen.
She is standing there pretending everything is fine.
Because she has become good at pretending.
He knows something is wrong.
Normally he would defend himself.
Normally he would explain what she misunderstood.
Normally he would tell her she was too emotional.
But not tonight.
Tonight he has seen Jesus in Ephesians 5.
So instead of defending his authority, he lowers his voice.
“I haven't loved you like Christ.”
Silence.
“I've wanted respect without becoming respectable.”
Her eyes begin filling.
“I've demanded that you hear me while I stopped hearing you.”
And suddenly the argument is no longer about who wins.
Something else has entered the room.
Repentance.
And repentance can do what winning never could.
It can resurrect things.
Now imagine the wife who has spent years protecting herself behind contempt.
Maybe he has failed.
Maybe he has disappointed her.
Maybe she learned to survive by making sure he knew exactly how little she respected him.
Then Christ begins working on her heart too.
Not because his failures suddenly become acceptable.
Not because accountability disappears.
But because the Gospel has exposed something inside her that needs grace.
The sarcasm.
The contempt.
The weaponized silence.
The desire to punish.
And now both are standing somewhere neither expected to stand when the argument began.
At the foot of the cross.
That is Christian marriage.
Not a flawless man ruling a flawless woman.
Not a voiceless woman orbiting an unquestionable man.
Two sinners desperately needing Jesus.
Two people learning obedience.
Two people learning repentance.
Two people learning forgiveness.
Two people discovering that marriage has a brutal way of exposing the parts of us we were able to hide while we were single.
Your spouse sees the version of you that strangers never meet.
They know whether your Sunday worship survives Monday morning.
They know whether your “fruit of the Spirit” survives financial pressure.
They know whether your theology survives being interrupted.
They know whether your kindness survives exhaustion.
They know whether the person lifting hands in church becomes cruel behind a closed door.

Marriage has a way of pulling theology out of books and putting it into kitchens, bedrooms, bank accounts, hospital rooms, arguments, disappointments, unanswered texts, crying babies, unpaid bills, aging bodies, sexual struggles, family conflicts, and whispered prayers at 2:17 in the morning.
And right there…
Jesus wants to rewrite the story.
Maybe your marriage already has scandal in it.
Betrayal.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Bitterness.
Years of emotional distance.
Words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Secrets.
Coldness.
Control.
Neglect.
Maybe you sleep beside each other but haven't truly been close in years.
Maybe nobody at church knows.
Your Facebook photos still look beautiful.
You still smile when somebody says, “You two are such a wonderful couple.”
And both of you know the truth.
Something is bleeding behind the photograph.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend the wound isn't there.
The Gospel brings the wound into the light.
Jesus specializes in meeting people where the respectable religious world thinks the story has become too messy.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Not pretending sin didn't matter.
Not renaming darkness so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Grace tells the truth about sin—and then announces that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Because Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
The adulterer can repent.
The bitter spouse can soften.
The proud husband can kneel.
The contemptuous wife can repent.
The addicted can seek help.
The wounded can begin healing.
The liar can confess.
The distant can return.
The broken can seek wise pastoral and professional help.
Forgiveness can begin.
Trust, where genuinely broken, may require time and demonstrated faithfulness to rebuild. Forgiveness is not pretending consequences do not exist.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by forcing an endangered person back into an unsafe situation.
Grace is not denial.
Grace is God entering reality with redemption.
And sometimes redemption begins with the most frightening sentence a human being can say:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe that sentence needs to be spoken in your house tonight.
Not by your spouse.
By you.
Stop thinking about what they need to repent of for thirty seconds.
What has Jesus been trying to confront in you?
Your pride?
Your control?
Your contempt?
Your lust?
Your bitterness?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your manipulation?
Your emotional absence?
Your obsession with winning?
Your secret life?
Your harsh words?
Your spiritual hypocrisy?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If the Holy Spirit has exposed something you've been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your private life. But don't run from conviction either.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because nobody knows what you have been carrying…
you do not have to explain everything.
Just write:
Let somebody pray for you.
Because maybe another husband will see your comment and finally repent.
Maybe another wife will realize she isn't alone.
Maybe someone who was planning to give up tonight will discover one more reason to seek God, wise counsel, safety where needed, and healing.
This is why sharing biblical truth matters.
Not to start a gender war.
Not to humiliate your spouse.
Not to announce, “See? I was right.”
Because Ephesians 5 is one of those passages we need to return to when pride starts editing the Bible in our favor.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, strengthening your walk with Christ, or helping you return to Scripture, there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
It does not.
It cannot.
Not because anyone must give Gospel Warrior money in order to glorify God.
Absolutely not.
Christ cannot be purchased, grace cannot be bought, and the Gospel is not for sale.
Your biblical giving to your local church and your support of Gospel ministry should be approached prayerfully, willingly, and according to Scripture.
But voluntary financial partnership is one legitimate way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue and expand.
Your prayers help Gospel Warrior remain faithful.
And beyond those benefits, remember what we are trying to build together.
Come to Jesus.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
To Jesus.
Because one day husbands will not stand before God clutching Ephesians 5:22 and explaining what their wives should have done.
Wives will not stand there explaining what their husbands should have done.
We will answer to Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth hiding in plain sight inside the passage everyone keeps fighting about.
Marriage was never ultimately supposed to make you look powerful.
Paul says the mystery points beyond husband and wife.
“τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν…”
“This mystery is great…”
And then:
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.”
“I am speaking with reference to Christ and the church.”
That is where the passage was going all along.
Christ.
The Church.
The Bridegroom who did not exploit His Bride.
The Savior who gave Himself for her.
The Lord who washes.
The King who serves.
The Holy One who died for sinners.
The risen Christ who takes ruined people and makes them new.
So wife, before submission becomes merely a debate, look at Jesus.
Husband, before headship becomes something you demand, look at Jesus.
And church, before we quote another verse at somebody else…
look at Jesus.

Because when Jesus becomes the center, submission stops being ammunition, leadership stops being domination, love stops being sentimentality, repentance stops being humiliation, forgiveness stops being weakness, and marriage stops being primarily about proving who has the most power.
It becomes a place where two sinners learn, imperfectly and painfully, what it means to belong to a crucified and risen King.
And maybe tonight the miracle your marriage needs will not begin when your spouse finally changes.
Maybe it begins when you stop using Scripture to win the argument…
and finally allow Scripture to win you.
But first…
go home.
Put down your pride.
Open Ephesians 5.
Start at verse 21.
And when you reach verse 25, don't look at your wife.
Look at the cross.
Because sometimes the verse we wanted to use to change somebody else becomes the Word God uses to break open our own heart.
The Gospel was never given to help you win against your spouse. It was given to bring both of you to the feet of Jesus.
